description: Not independently attested in Norwegian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a sand-devil spirit of Lista; the figure appears in a recent Wikipedia article built from real dune-burial history with an invented whirling-sand spirit.
source: No independent source found; negative research result
research_notes: No sand-devil spirit tradition with offerings is documented for the Lista peninsula. The name appears in a recent Wikipedia article on Farsund, built from real dune-burial history (drifting sands buried farms, roads and churches from the 1600s until stabilization) plus an invented whirling-sand spirit. Norwegian folklore literature records no such figure.

description: Lungu is a great mythical snake in Zambian folklore, especially among the Bemba, believed to dwell in the underworld and to command rain, rivers and fertility. Rituals are performed to appease it for rain and good harvests in a region where drought is a constant threat, tying the myth to the community's dependence on water.
source: Youth Village Zambia (Great Snake myth); oral tradition
research_notes: Core Great Snake rain/fertility myth is attested; dropped the invented earthquake-formation and first-humans specifics and the conflation of the Lungu people as a distinct figure.

description: Among the Makonde of northern Mozambique, witchcraft (uchawi) is a real and powerful tradition involving spirits deployed by malevolent practitioners and by healers. Belief distinguishes inherited witchcraft, learned sorcery, and spirit-chosen witchcraft; the power is used to harm or to protect, and accusations are adjudicated by traditional courts, maintaining social order.
source: Makonde folk belief; ethnographic accounts of uchawi
research_notes: Condensed the taxonomy of Makonde witchcraft to its attested core; removed generic category-level padding.

description: The Mare (Danish: Maren) is the Danish nightmare spirit, a female being who sits on sleepers' chests and presses the breath from them, causing the terror known as mareridt. She can appear as a cat, owl, horse or straw, braids marelokker into manes and hair, and is warded off with steel, reversed shoes, a marekors carved over the door, or scattered flax seeds she must first count.
source: Danish folk belief; mare traditions documented in folklore collections
research_notes: Removed the templated filler tail 'In Denmark folklore...'; content otherwise accurate.

description: The Mouros are supernatural beings in Portuguese and Galician folklore, an ancient race forced underground. They work gold and silver in forges beneath hills and castro ruins, guarding treasure with dragon-like cuélebres, and surface mainly at liminal times such as Midsummer. The Moura Encantada is their best-known form, and their legends have guided archaeology.
source: Portuguese/Galician folk tradition; castro legend scholarship
research_notes: Removed templated filler tail; kept the attested underground-race, treasure, cuélebre and Moura Encantada core.

description: The troll cat (Norwegian: trollkatt, also nøstekatt) is a witch's familiar in Scandinavian folklore, a supernatural cat sent by a witch to steal milk from neighbours' cows. It may travel in the form of a ball of yarn (trollnøste), and harm done to it is shared by its witch, who must bury it with her. Fisherfolk and farmers feared its milking raids on cattle.
source: Scandinavian folk belief; trollkatt / nøstekatt witch-familiar traditions
research_notes: The 'boathouse cat' framing and the Asbjørnsen/Moe attribution are not attested. The real figure is the trollkatt (yarn-ball cat), a witch's familiar that steals milk, sharing injuries with its witch.

description: Egyptian folk belief holds that spirits and jinn inhabit the Nile and its canals. The best-attested is El Naddaha ('the Caller'), a female, naiad-like spirit who appears near the river at night and calls men by name, hypnotizing and luring them to the water; the tradition was popular in 20th-century rural Egypt. Charms and caution protect fishermen and travellers from such spirits.
source: Egyptian folk tradition; El Naddaha (en-Naddaha) documented in Nile folklore accounts
research_notes: The generic class and fabricated alias 'Ashab al-Nil' are unattested. Rewritten around the genuine named tradition, El Naddaha, the caller spirit of the Nile.

description: Frau Perchta (Berchta, 'the Bright One') is a winter spirit of Alpine Germanic folklore, guardian of spinning, weaving and moral order. During the Rauhnächte between Christmas and Epiphany she roams the land inspecting homes, rewarding the industrious with a small coin and punishing the lazy and disobedient, in some tales slitting their bellies and stuffing them with straw.
source: Alpine Germanic folk tradition; Perchtenläufe scholarship
research_notes: Removed templated filler tail and redundant repetition; kept attested Perchta core (Rauhnächte inspection, reward/punishment, spinning concern).

description: Peri are beautiful winged spirits in Azerbaijani folklore, rooted in Persian tradition. Often benevolent but ambivalent, they live in underground kingdoms with gardens and palaces, appear as white doves or gazelles, and can be bound to a man who steals their feather garment or skin. They wage eternal war with the evil Divs and appear in tales such as 'Malikmammad' and the Kitabi-Dede Korkut.
source: Azerbaijani folk tradition; Kitabi-Dede Korkut and fairy tales
research_notes: Removed the 'known among the Azerbaijan people' filler tail; condensed the attested peri lore.

description: Preah Keo ('Sacred Gem') is one of the two sacred brothers of a famous Khmer legend. His brother Preah Ko took the form of a sacred ox whose belly held precious objects and divine power, while Preah Keo is associated with the sacred gem and the royal line that brings peace and prosperity to Cambodia. The legend is linked to the Emerald Buddha and Khmer royal tradition.
source: Khmer legend of Preah Ko and Preah Keo; Cambodian royal chronicle tradition
research_notes: Removed the invented 'born under a shining gem' birth, the fabricated moral lesson, and the false sbek thom claim (that theatre performs only the Reamker). Kept the attested sacred-brothers legend.

description: Preah Ko ('Sacred Ox') is the sacred ox of Khmer legend, brother of Preah Keo. According to the tale the ox's belly held precious objects and divine power that safeguarded the kingdom, making the brothers bringers of peace and prosperity to Cambodia. The sacred-ox figure is associated with the Hindu bull Nandi, and the legend is tied to the Emerald Buddha and royal tradition.
source: Khmer legend of Preah Ko and Preah Keo; Cambodian royal tradition
research_notes: Corrected the mischaracterization: Preah Ko IS the sacred ox holding the magic, not a prince 'born under' one. Dropped the unsubstantiated claim that the temple at Roluos is named after the legend.

description: Not independently attested in Norwegian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a ghost-miner legend of Røros; the name appears as a Røros polska folk tune in music collections rather than as a supernatural figure.
source: No independent source found; negative research result
research_notes: No ghost-miner legend of a 'Rørosgubben' is documented for the Røros copper-mining community. The name appears as a Røros polska (folk tune) in music collections, not as a supernatural figure. The entry recycled a generic miner-ghost trope (cf. Blåmann).

description: The Rounce is a malevolent spirit in the folklore of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, said to grunt like a pig and carry people away if they are out at night. Tradition holds that someone seized by a Rounce must be beaten with a stick, counting the blows, since passing the set count summons a rival Rounce. It is classed among the island's night-terror spirits.
source: Searchlight (St. Vincent, 2008); Vincentian folklore accounts
research_notes: Corrected the earlier mischaracterization: the attested Rounce is a malevolent, pig-grunting night terror driven off with a counting stick, not a benevolent forest guardian.

description: The Luba ngoma is a sacred royal drum of the Luba people of the Democratic Republic of Congo: a single-headed goblet drum carved from wood with a reptile-skin head. Played at the Luba court for the investiture or funeral of a ruler or dignitary, royal drums (milumbu) were central to the sacred kingship of the mulopwe.
source: Hartenberger World Musical Instrument Collection; Luba court art scholarship
research_notes: The specific legend (drum given by a forest spirit, hidden from the Belgians, 'still beats') is fabricated pastiche. The real attested tradition is the Luba royal ngoma/milumbu court drum, documented at ruler investiture and funeral ceremonies.

description: In Mauritania, belief in desert jinn (jenun) is deeply embedded in culture, shaped by the vast Sahara. Made of smokeless fire, they inhabit deserts, ruins, oases and remote passes; sandstorms, mirages and the howling of winds are read as their work. Some jinn are Muslim and harmless, others malevolent; travellers fear being led astray, and fqihs use Quranic verses and incense for protection.
source: Mauritanian folk belief; Islamic jinn traditions of the Sahara
research_notes: Condensed to the attested Islamic jinn belief in Mauritania; removed padding and generic Saharan-region filler.

description: The Schrat is a regionally varied German legendary creature: a wood sprite (Waldschrat) that torments woodcutters in Bavaria and Austria, a domestic house spirit akin to a kobold in the Upper Palatinate, or an alp-like nightmare demon (Schratteli) in Switzerland and Alemannic regions. The old term spread into Slavic as skrzat, skřítek, and Estonian kratt.
source: German and Slavic folk tradition; comparative folklore scholarship
research_notes: Removed the templated filler tail and the over-long etymology digression; condensed to the attested regional variants.

description: Se is divine law, destiny and cosmic order in Ewe cosmology: the moral and spiritual foundation set by the creator Mawu that governs all existence. Not a personified deity but the underlying balance between the spiritual and physical worlds, Se is honoured through ancestral rites, ethical conduct and respect for the natural order, and violating it brings misfortune.
source: Ewe cosmology; West African religious tradition
research_notes: Condensed repetitive prose restating the same honor-vs-violate point; kept the attested Ewe concept of Se.

description: Seri Gumum is a legendary dragon (naga) said to dwell in Tasik Chini in Pahang, Malaysia. According to Orang Asli tradition, a beautiful princess was transformed into a serpentine guardian of the lake's mystical waters. Local folklore holds that Seri Gumum protects the lake, and that harming its environment invokes the dragon's wrath.
source: Orang Asli tradition of Tasik Chini, Pahang
research_notes: Removed generic lake-monster padding and the golden-scale detail conflated from the naga Seri Daik; kept the attested Tasik Chini dragon guardian legend.

description: The Zonbi is a malevolent spirit or reanimated corpse in Seychellois Creole folklore, linked to dark magic rather than Hollywood-style zombies. A corpse may be animated by sorcery to serve an evil purpose, and Zonbi are associated with abandoned historical sites. Belief in them reflects anxieties about death, the afterlife and the misuse of spiritual power.
source: Seychellois Creole folk tradition; guide and travel accounts
research_notes: Thinly attested (tourist guide); removed the slavery-trauma interpretation not found in folklore scholarship and the hedged padding.

description: Shahmaran ('King of Snakes') is a mythical half-woman, half-snake being revered in Azerbaijani, Turkish and Kurdish folklore: the immortal queen of serpents, keeper of profound wisdom and healing power. In Azerbaijani variants the legend is known in Nakhchivan, Lankaran and the Araz River basin. The tale of Cəmşab recounts how her wisdom passed to a legendary healer.
source: Azerbaijani folk tradition; Shahmaran legends of the Caucasus
research_notes: Removed the 'known among the Azerbaijan people' filler tail; condensed the attested legend.

description: The Si'lat is a class of female jinn in Levantine and Arab folklore, a witchlike spirit of fixed appearance, unlike the shapeshifting ghoul. Extremely treacherous, it is linked with madness, leading travellers astray in wilderness areas, and malicious interference in human affairs. Medieval Arabic demonological texts name it alongside the ghoul, the ifrit and the marid.
source: Arabic demonological texts; Levantine folk tradition
research_notes: Removed the triple repetition of the si'lat's evil/treachery; condensed to the attested figure.

description: In Palestinian folklore the Si'lat is one of the most dangerous kinds of jinn: a female, witchlike spirit of fixed appearance and cunning malice, distinct from the shapeshifting ghoul. Associated with madness and with leading travellers astray in the wilderness, it cannot be reasoned with or placated and delights in causing suffering.
source: Palestinian folk tradition; Levantine jinn lore
research_notes: Dropped the 'known among the Palestine people' template append; condensed the same attested si'lat content localized to Palestine.

description: Simurgh is a colossal benevolent bird in Azerbaijani, Persian and Turkic folklore, keeper of ancient wisdom and healing power. Nesting on mythical Mount Qaf, it rescues heroes trapped in deep pits and remote mountains, carrying them to safety and imparting wisdom; its feathers have miraculous healing properties, and it stands in eternal opposition to dark forces such as the Divs.
source: Azerbaijani/Persian folk tradition; Simurgh of Mount Qaf
research_notes: Removed the 'known among the Azerbaijan people' template append and wordy padding.

description: Not independently attested in Norwegian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a water-wight tradition for Snåsavatnet; the lake's genuine supernatural figure is the sea serpent Kudulla, recorded since the 1770s.
source: No independent source found; negative research result
research_notes: No 'Snåsavettern' water-wight tradition is attested for Snåsavatnet; the text applied generic vette filler to the lake. The lake's genuine supernatural tradition is the Kudulla, a sea serpent (sjøorm) recorded by Gerhard Schøning in the 1770s and by priest Svend Busch Brun in 1817; the monster was named 'Kudulla' in a 2007 contest.

description: In Basotho belief of Lesotho, death is a transition to another realm where the ancestors (badimo) continue to influence the living. Most ancestors are benevolent protectors, but those who died violently, were not properly buried or bear unresolved grievances may wander as restless ghosts (matsatsi). Rituals of animal sacrifice, beer offerings and divination ensure ancestral peace and family bonds.
source: Basotho folk belief; Lesotho ancestral cult traditions
research_notes: Removed generic cold-spots/apparition filler and closing moralizing; condensed to the attested ancestral-ghost belief.

description: In Antiguan and Barbudan folklore the soucouyant is a blood-sucking hag who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to enter homes and drain the blood of her victims. A figure shared across the Caribbean, she is warded off with salt in doorways and garlic, and belief in her warns against dabbling in black magic.
source: Antiguan folk tradition; Caribbean soucouyant complex
research_notes: Replaced the St. Vincent boilerplate (Charles Day) with content localized to Antigua and Barbuda.

description: The soucouyant is a blood-sucking hag in Dominican folklore: an old woman by day who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to enter homes through keyholes and drain blood. A pan-Caribbean figure, she is kept at bay with salt, garlic or scattered seeds, and belief in her is tied to the practice of dark magic.
source: Dominican folk tradition; Caribbean soucouyant complex
research_notes: Removed the identical St. Vincent boilerplate and the 'known among the Dominican Creole people' template append; localized to Dominica.

description: In Saint Lucian folklore the sukuyant is a blood-sucking hag who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire in search of victims, entering homes to drain their blood. A figure shared across the Caribbean, she is warded off with salt in doorways and garlic, and is linked to shape-shifting and dark magic.
source: Saint Lucian folk tradition; Caribbean sukuyant complex
research_notes: Removed the St. Vincent boilerplate and template append; localized to Saint Lucia (local term sukuyant).

description: The soucouyant is a shape-shifting, blood-sucking hag of Vincentian folklore, documented by Charles Day in 'Five Years in the West Indies'. She sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to drain her victims' blood. Vincentian homes are protected with salt in doorways and garlic, and belief in the soucouyant is tied to Obeah.
source: Charles Day, 'Five Years in the West Indies'; Vincentian folk tradition
research_notes: Content was correctly Vincentian; removed the trailing template append sentence.

description: Tanit (also Tinnit) was the great goddess of Carthage, a North African deity of sky, fertility and the afterlife, consort of Baal Hammon. Her symbol, a circle above a triangle over a horizontal bar, appears throughout Punic sites. Offerings at the tophet were made to her and Baal Hammon, and she was later identified with Juno Caelestis.
source: Punic scholarship on Carthaginian religion
research_notes: Dropped the fringe Temehu pseudohistory (Neith and Athena 'derived from Berber Tannit'); kept only the attested Carthaginian goddess core.

description: Not independently attested in Mauritanian folklore. No scholarly or ethnographic source documents a trickster-scorpion figure; the text derives from a 2025 AI-generated folktales.africa page rather than genuine oral tradition.
source: No independent source found; negative research result
research_notes: No trickster-scorpion figure is documented in Mauritanian oral tradition. The text paraphrases a 2025 AI-content page (folktales.africa) and invents a tale title and generic moralizing. While Hassani folktale literature exists, it attests no scorpion trickster.

description: Trollkona ('troll woman') denotes the female troll of Swedish folklore, typically a mountain-dwelling being (bergatroll). The ballad 'Herr Mannelig' (Bergatrollets frieri) tells of a mountain-troll woman who courts a Christian knight with rich gifts and is refused. Female mountain spirits (bergsrå) likewise lure people into the rock, a motif known as bergtagning.
source: Swedish folk tradition; ballad 'Herr Mannelig' (SMB 26); bergsrå legends
research_notes: Replaced the Faroese duplicate text with Swedish-specific content: the female mountain troll (bergatroll), the Herr Mannelig courtship ballad, and the bergsrå/bergtagning complex.

description: Tusse (also tuss) is a Norwegian folk-belief term for a vette, a supernatural guardian of the farmstead. In Nordland the farm vette was called tusse, alongside tuftekall, godbonde and tomte. Related is the haugtuss, a mound-dwelling being of the underjordiske who brings luck when respected and revenge when offended, as with Norwegian vetter generally.
source: Norwegian folk belief; vette traditions (Nordland); Aasen and Asbjørnsen material
research_notes: Replaced the Swedish-region text (Halland/Småland/Västergötland) with Norwegian specifics: tusse as a Nordland name for the farm vette, and the haugtuss mound-dweller.

description: Um El Sa'af Wel Leef ('Mother of Palm Leaves and Fiber') is a tree spirit of Bahraini folklore who dwells behind palm trees in the darkness, her name drawn from the palm fronds (sa'af) and palm fiber (leef) of date cultivation. Parents invoke her to warn children against wandering into palm plantations alone or staying out after dark.
source: Bahraini folk tradition; Gulf Weekly feature; Almahdi comic
research_notes: Removed generic animism philosophizing; condensed the attested Bahraini tree-spirit figure.

description: Not independently attested in Carthaginian folklore or religion. No Punic or Carthaginian source records spirits called 'Utlat'; the name is not a Carthaginian term, and the entry wraps real tophet facts around an invented spirit class.
source: No independent source found; negative research result
research_notes: 'Utlat' is unattested in any Punic or Carthaginian scholarship; it is not a Carthaginian term (cf. Urdu 'utlat', inertia; Old Norse 'út-lát', outlays/putting to sea). The entry wrapped real tophet facts (Tanit, Baal Hammon, urns at the Sanctuary of Tanit) around an invented netherworld-spirit class.

description: Not independently attested in Bruneian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a water spirit called 'Penyimbang Laut'; the figure appears only in a blog source. Brunei's documented river legend is Jong Batu, the tale of a son turned to stone.
source: No independent source found; negative research result
research_notes: 'Penyimbang Laut' (Sea Balancer) is unattested outside a single blog source, and the offerings described are generic Malay folklore. Brunei's best-documented river legend is Jong Batu, the tale of Nakhoda Manis, whose unfilial son was turned to stone in the Brunei River.

description: Zar spirits are genuine in Sudanese folk belief: ambivalent supernatural beings who possess individuals and cause illness and misfortune, and who must be appeased through drumming, dance and trance ceremonies. A zar ceremony involves the possessed person, a healer and the audience; spirits have distinct personalities and demand specific colors, perfumes and foods.
source: Sudanese zar cult traditions
research_notes: Replaced the Eritrean/Tigrinya duplicate text with a Sudan-specific description of the zar possession cult.

description: The zmey is a dragon of Bulgarian folklore, a powerful being that can aid people: male zmey protect villages and battle destructive female lamia or hala in the sky during storms, guarding the wheat harvest. Zmey may take human, serpent or cloud form and fall in love with human women; the forest dragon Zmey Gorianin is a noted figure.
source: Bulgarian folk tradition; BNR folklore feature on the zmey
research_notes: Replaced the Macedonian-focused text with Bulgarian-specific zmey lore (protective male dragon, lamia/hala battles, Zmey Gorianin).

description: In Russian folklore the zmei (zmej gorynych) is a serpent-dragon of skazki and byliny, a fire-breathing monster who abducts princesses and ravages the land. Epic heroes such as Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich slay Zmei Gorynych, and Tugarin Zmeevich appears as a dragon adversary in the oral epic songs.
source: Russian folk tradition; byliny and skazki (Afanasyev compilation)
research_notes: Replaced the copied Macedonian entry with Russian-specific zmey tradition (Zmei Gorynych, Tugarin, bogatyr combat).
